why_use_this:
Reach for `BigInt` the moment an integer computation might overflow `i64` -- vāṇी's native integers trap (a hard runtime error) rather than wrap on overflow, and there is no wider native integer type, so exact factorials, large combinatorics, cryptographic-scale numbers, or any computation whose intermediate values you can't bound in advance need this package instead. `BigInt` stores digits as little-endian base-1e9 limbs and is NOT a Copy type (it owns a `Vec<i64>`), so every function takes `ref`/`mut ref BigInt` and returns a fresh `BigInt` by value -- budget for that allocation cost, unlike the Copy-struct sibling libraries ([vani-complex](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-complex), [vani-interval](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-interval)). Despite what the README's "What's included" table currently says ("v0.1.0 -- integers only... Rational numbers... Not started"), this package (now at v0.2.0) actually DOES include a full `Rational` type (`rat_*` functions: construction, arithmetic, comparison, all reduced via `bn_gcd` to lowest terms) built on top of `BigInt` -- reach for `Rational` specifically when you need EXACT fractions with no floating-point rounding at all (`1/3 + 1/3 + 1/3` genuinely equals `1`, not something that merely rounds to it).

`BigInt` stores a number as a sequence of "limbs", each holding up to 9 decimal digits (base \(10^9\)), least-significant limb first -- exactly like ordinary decimal digits, just with a much bigger "digit" than 0-9. A few of the examples below use a smaller base (10) instead of the real base (\(10^9\)) purely so the numbers stay hand-sized -- the carrying/borrowing mechanics are identical either way, just with more digits per limb in the real implementation.

bn_add.intuition: Adding two big numbers works exactly like the addition you learned in grade school, just with each "column" holding up to 9 digits (a whole limb) instead of 1. Add the two numbers' limbs position by position; whenever a column's sum reaches or exceeds the base, carry the overflow into the next column, same as carrying a 1 when adding 7+5 in ordinary decimal.
bn_add.formula: Add magnitudes limb-by-limb with carry propagation (base \(10^9\) per limb) when signs match; when signs differ, subtract the smaller magnitude from the larger and take the sign of whichever operand has the bigger magnitude.
bn_add.example: Add \(123{,}456{,}789 + 987{,}654{,}321\). Both fit in one limb each (each under \(10^9\)): limb sum \(=123456789+987654321=1{,}111{,}111{,}110\). That's \(\ge 10^9\), so it doesn't fit in one limb: subtract the base to get this limb's digits, \(1{,}111{,}111{,}110 - 1{,}000{,}000{,}000 = 111{,}111{,}110\), and carry \(1\) into the next limb. Result: limb0\(=111{,}111{,}110\), limb1\(=1\) -- representing \(1\times10^9 + 111{,}111{,}110 = 1{,}111{,}111{,}110\), which is exactly the correct sum.
bn_add.why: This carry step is the ENTIRE reason `BigInt` needs more than one `i64` in the first place: a sum that overflows one limb just grows into a second limb instead of overflowing and trapping the way a plain `i64 + i64` would once the true sum exceeds what 64 bits can hold.

bn_sub.intuition: Rather than writing a whole separate borrowing algorithm for subtraction, this package reuses addition: \(a-b\) is the same as \(a+(-b)\), so subtraction is really just "negate the second operand, then add" -- one algorithm to get right and reuse, instead of two.
bn_sub.example: Compute \(10-3\): negate \(3\) to get \(-3\), then add: \(10 + (-3)\). Since the signs now differ, `bn_add`'s subtract-the-smaller-magnitude branch kicks in: \(|10|-|-3| = 10-3=7\), taking the sign of the larger-magnitude operand (positive, since \(10>3\)). Result: \(7\), correctly.
bn_sub.why: This is a small but real design choice worth noticing: it means `bn_sub` can never have its own bug independent of `bn_neg`/`bn_add` -- any correctness proof or test for addition automatically covers subtraction too.

bn_mul.intuition: Long multiplication, generalized the same way `bn_add` generalizes addition: multiply every limb of one number against every limb of the other, and add up all the partial products, carrying as you go -- exactly the grade-school "multiply by each digit, shift, add" procedure, just with base-\(10^9\) limbs instead of base-10 digits.
bn_mul.formula: Schoolbook \(O(n\cdot m)\) multiplication: every limb of \(a\) times every limb of \(b\), accumulated with carries.
bn_mul.example: For a hand-sized example, use BASE 10 (ordinary digits) instead of base \(10^9\) -- the mechanics are identical either way. Multiply \(23\times14\), with \(23\) as digits \([3,2]\) (least significant first) and \(14\) as digits \([4,1]\): units-times-units: \(3\times4=12\) -- write down \(2\), carry \(1\). Cross terms: \(3\times1 + 2\times4 = 3+8=11\), plus the carried \(1\) makes \(12\) -- write down \(2\), carry \(1\). Tens-times-tens: \(2\times1=2\), plus the carried \(1\) makes \(3\). Reading the digits from most to least significant: \(3,2,2\), i.e. \(322\) -- matching \(23\times14=322\) exactly.
bn_mul.why: This costs \(O(n\cdot m)\) limb-multiplications for an \(n\)-limb times \(m\)-limb number -- fine for numbers up to a few hundred digits, but genuinely slower than it needs to be for VERY large numbers (cryptographic-scale, thousands of digits), where Karatsuba or FFT-based multiplication would asymptotically win -- a deliberate "simplest correct choice" tradeoff this package makes, matching the same choice this ecosystem makes elsewhere (see [vani-discrete](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-discrete)'s Floyd-Warshall-not-Johnson's precedent).

bn_div_mod.intuition: Division and remainder are computed together because long division naturally produces both at once -- by the time you know how many times the divisor goes into the dividend, you also already know what's left over. The one subtlety worth knowing: this TRUNCATES toward zero, the same convention vāṇी's native `/`/`%` use, which is NOT the same as mathematical floor division once negative numbers are involved.
bn_div_mod.formula: Quotient sign is \(\text{sign}(a)\cdot\text{sign}(b)\); remainder sign matches \(a\)'s sign; truncating (rounding the quotient toward zero, not toward negative infinity).
bn_div_mod.example: \(17 \div 5\): quotient \(3\) (since \(5\times3=15\le17\)), remainder \(17-15=2\). Now try a NEGATIVE case, \(-17\div5\): truncating toward zero gives quotient \(-3\) (not \(-4\), which is what FLOOR division would give), and remainder \(-17 - 5\times(-3) = -17+15=-2\) -- negative, matching \(a=-17\)'s own sign, per the stated convention.
bn_div_mod.why: If you're used to a language whose `%` always returns a non-negative result (Python's, for instance), this truncating convention can surprise you: \(-17 \bmod 5\) is \(-2\) here, not \(3\). This is a deliberate match to vāṇी's own native integer semantics, not an oversight -- code moving between plain `i64` arithmetic and `BigInt` arithmetic gets the same rounding behavior either way.

bn_gcd.intuition: The Euclidean algorithm is one of the oldest algorithms known, and still the simplest way to find the greatest common divisor: repeatedly replace the pair \((a,b)\) with \((b, a\bmod b)\) -- the remainder of dividing the bigger by the smaller -- and keep going. Every step preserves the pair's gcd exactly, and the numbers shrink fast, so it always finishes quickly.
bn_gcd.example: Find \(\gcd(48,18)\). Step 1: \(48 \bmod 18 = 12\) (since \(18\times2=36\), remainder \(12\)) -- new pair \((18,12)\). Step 2: \(18\bmod12=6\) -- new pair \((12,6)\). Step 3: \(12\bmod6=0\) -- new pair \((6,0)\). Since the second element is now \(0\), the answer is the first: \(\gcd(48,18)=6\). Check: \(48=6\times8\), \(18=6\times3\), and \(8,3\) share no common factor -- confirmed.
bn_gcd.why: Every `rat_*` constructor calls this to reduce a fraction to lowest terms (e.g. turning \(48/18\) into \(8/3\) by dividing both by this same \(\gcd=6\)) -- without it, repeated arithmetic on rationals would let numerators and denominators grow unboundedly even when the actual VALUE stays simple.

bn_pow_i64.intuition: Computing \(a^n\) by multiplying \(a\) by itself \(n-1\) times works, but wastes effort: repeated SQUARING gets there in far fewer multiplications, by building up \(a^1, a^2, a^4, a^8, \ldots\) (each just the previous one squared) and combining only the ones whose exponent corresponds to a 1-bit in \(n\)'s binary representation.
bn_pow_i64.formula: Exponentiation by repeated squaring: \(O(\log n)\) multiplications instead of \(n-1\).
bn_pow_i64.example: Compute \(3^5\). Write \(5\) in binary: \(101_2 = 4+1\). Build the squares: \(3^1=3\), \(3^2=9\), \(3^4=81\) (squaring \(3^2\)). The bits of \(5\) that are 1 correspond to exponents \(4\) and \(1\), so combine those: \(3^5 = 3^4\times3^1 = 81\times3=243\). Only 3 multiplications total (to get \(3^2\), \(3^4\), and the final combine) instead of the 4 multiplications naive repeated multiplication would need -- a small saving here, but the gap widens fast: computing \(3^{1000}\) needs about 10-11 squarings this way instead of 999 multiplications.
bn_pow_i64.why: For `BigInt` specifically, where each individual multiplication can itself be expensive (numbers with hundreds or thousands of digits), the difference between \(O(\log n)\) and \(O(n)\) multiplications is often the difference between a computation finishing instantly and one that doesn't finish in a reasonable time at all.

bn_pow_mod.intuition: Computing \(a^n\) first and THEN reducing modulo \(m\) would work mathematically, but for large \(n\) the intermediate value \(a^n\) can become astronomically larger than \(m\) ever needs it to be -- wasted work computing digits that get thrown away by the final modulo. Reducing modulo \(m\) after EVERY multiplication in the repeated-squaring process keeps every intermediate value bounded by \(m\), never letting it grow larger than necessary.
bn_pow_mod.formula: Same repeated-squaring structure as `bn_pow_i64`, but every intermediate product is reduced modulo \(m\) immediately: \((a\cdot b)\bmod m\) computed at each step, never the full unreduced product.
bn_pow_mod.example: Compute \(3^5 \bmod 7\), reducing at every step: \(3^1\bmod7=3\). \(3^2\bmod7 = 9\bmod7=2\) (reduced immediately, never carrying the full 9 forward). \(3^4\bmod7 = 2^2\bmod7=4\bmod7=4\) (squaring the ALREADY-REDUCED value 2, not 81). Combine using the same bit pattern as before (\(5=101_2\), exponents 4 and 1): \(3^5\bmod7 = (3^4\bmod7)\times(3^1\bmod7)\bmod7 = 4\times3\bmod7=12\bmod7=5\). Double-check against the unreduced answer: \(3^5=243\), and \(243=7\times34+5\), so \(243\bmod7=5\) -- matches, but this way, none of the intermediate numbers ever exceeded \(7^2=49\), versus the unreduced path's \(243\).
bn_pow_mod.why: This difference matters enormously at cryptographic scale: computing something like \(a^{2048}\bmod m\) for a 2048-bit \(m\) directly (compute the full power, then reduce) would produce an intermediate number with millions of digits; reducing at every squaring step keeps every intermediate value the same size as \(m\) itself, which is the entire reason modular exponentiation is computationally feasible at all.

rat_new.intuition: A fraction like \(6/8\) and \(3/4\) represent the same VALUE, but as different pairs of numbers -- for equality comparisons and predictable behavior, it's much simpler if every `Rational` this package ever produces is already in its one canonical simplest form, so two equal values are always represented IDENTICALLY, not just equal after simplification.
rat_new.formula: Divide both numerator and denominator by \(\gcd(|\text{num}|,|\text{den}|)\) (via `bn_gcd`), and normalize the sign onto the numerator so the denominator is always positive.
rat_new.example: Construct the rational \(6/8\): \(\gcd(6,8)=2\) (from `bn_gcd`'s example pattern: \(8\bmod6=2\), \(6\bmod2=0\), so \(\gcd=2\)). Divide both by \(2\): \(6/2=3\), \(8/2=4\). Result: \(3/4\), already in lowest terms.
rat_new.why: Because EVERY `Rational` this package produces is already reduced this way, `rat_eq` can just compare numerator-to-numerator and denominator-to-denominator directly -- it never needs to cross-multiply to check equality, because two rationals with the same value are guaranteed to already have identical numerators and denominators, not just equal ones after further simplification.

rat_add.intuition: Adding fractions with different denominators needs a common denominator first -- the standard trick is to multiply each fraction by a form of 1 (the other fraction's denominator over itself) so both share the denominator \(bd\), then add the numerators directly.
rat_add.formula: \[ \dfrac{a}{b} + \dfrac{c}{d} = \dfrac{ad+cb}{bd} \] then reduced to lowest terms by `rat_new`.
rat_add.example: Compute \(1/2 + 1/3\): \(\dfrac{1\times3 + 1\times2}{2\times3} = \dfrac{3+2}{6} = \dfrac{5}{6}\). Since \(\gcd(5,6)=1\), this is already in lowest terms -- `rat_new` leaves it unchanged.
rat_add.why: Every step here uses `BigInt` arithmetic throughout (the cross-multiplications, the addition, the final gcd-reduction), so this is EXACT -- unlike adding `1.0/2.0 + 1.0/3.0` as floating-point numbers, which introduces rounding error, `rat_add` never loses precision no matter how many times you chain additions together.

rat_sub.intuition: The same cross-multiplication idea as `rat_add`, with subtraction instead of addition in the numerator.
rat_sub.why: Like `rat_add`, every intermediate value is exact `BigInt` arithmetic -- no floating-point rounding creeps in even after many chained subtractions.

rat_mul.intuition: Multiplying fractions doesn't need a common denominator at all -- just multiply the numerators together and the denominators together directly, the simplest of the four fraction operations.
rat_mul.example: Compute \(2/3 \times 3/4\): numerators \(2\times3=6\), denominators \(3\times4=12\), giving \(6/12\) BEFORE reduction. `rat_new` then reduces: \(\gcd(6,12)=6\), so \(6/12 \to 1/2\).
rat_mul.why: Notice the un-reduced intermediate \(6/12\) shares an obvious factor of 6 with itself, coming from the \(3\) in the first fraction's denominator cancelling against the \(3\) in the second fraction's numerator -- `rat_new`'s automatic reduction catches exactly this kind of cancellation without the caller needing to spot it by hand.

rat_div.intuition: Dividing by a fraction is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal (flip numerator and denominator) -- "how many quarters fit in a half" is the same question as "a half times four".
rat_div.example: Compute \((1/2) \div (1/3)\): flip the second fraction to \(3/1\) and multiply: \(\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{3}{1} = \dfrac{3}{2}\). Sanity check: \(3/2 = 1.5\), and indeed a half divided by a third (\(0.5 \div 0.333\ldots\)) is \(1.5\).
rat_div.why: The divisor rational must be nonzero for this to be defined -- dividing by the rational zero (\(0/1\)) is exactly as undefined as dividing an ordinary integer by zero, and for the same reason: there's no fraction you could multiply zero by to get back a nonzero numerator.
